Adrien Dubouloz Address: Institut de Mathématiques de Bourgogne, 9 avenue Alain Savary, 21 078 Dijon, France Email address: adrien.dubouloz@u-bourgogne.fr and Takashi Kishimoto Address: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science, Saitama University, Saitama 338-8570, Japan Email address: tkishimo@rimath.saitama-u.ac.jp
Abstract.

A classical result of Miyanishi-Sugie and Keel-Mckernan asserts that for smooth affine surfaces, 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruledness is equivalent to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness, both properties being in fact equivalent to the negativity of the logarithmic Kodaira dimension. Here we show in contrast that starting from dimension three, there exists smooth affine varieties which are 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled but not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled.

Introduction

Complex uniruled projective varieties are nowadays considered through the Mori Minimal Model Program (MMP) as the natural generalization to higher dimensions of birationaly ruled surfaces (see e.g. [12]). In particular, as in the case of ruled surfaces, these are the varieties for which the program does not yield a minimal model, but a Mori fiber space. These varieties are also conjectured to be the natural generalization to higher dimensions of surfaces of negative Kodaira dimension, the conjecture being in fact established as long as the abundance conjecture holds true [11], hence in particular for smooth threefolds. During the past decades, the systematic study of the geometry of rational curves on these varieties has been the source of many progress in the structure theory for higher dimensional, possibly singular, projective varieties to which the MMP can be applied. The situation is much less clear for non complete varieties, in particular affine ones.

The natural analogue of ruledness in this context is the notion of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness, a variety XX being called 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled if it contains a Zariski dense open subset UU of the form U≃𝔸1×YU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y for a suitable quasi-projective variety YY. A landmark result of Miyanishi-Sugie [14] asserts that a smooth affine surface is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled if and only if it has negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension [6]. For such surfaces, the projection prY:U≃𝔸1×Y→Y\mathrm{pr}_{Y}:U\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y\rightarrow Y always extends to a fibration p:X→Zp:X\rightarrow Z with general fibers isomorphic to the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} over an open subset of the smooth projective model of YY, providing the affine counterpart of the fact that a smooth birationaly ruled projective surface has the structure of a fibration with general fibers isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} over a smooth projective curve. This result, together with the description of the geometry of degenerate fibers of these fibrations, has been one of the cornerstones of the structure theory of smooth affine surfaces developed during the past decades. But in contrast, the foundations for a systematic study of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine threefolds have been only laid recently in [5]. On the other hand, from the point of view of logarithmic Kodaira dimension, the appropriate counterpart of the notion of uniruledness for a non necessarily complete variety XX is to require that XX is generically covered by images of the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, in the sense that the set of points x∈Xx\in X with the property that there exists a non constant morphism f=fx:𝔸1→Xf=f_{x}:\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X such that x∈fx​(𝔸1)x\in f_{x}(\mathbb{A}^{1}) is dense in XX with respect to the Zariski topology. Such varieties are called 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled, or log-uniruled after Keel and McKernan [8], and can be equivalently characterized by the property that they admit an open embedding into a complete variety X¯\overline{X} which is covered by proper rational curves meeting the boundary X¯∖X\overline{X}\setminus X in at most one point. In particular, a smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled quasi-projective variety XX has negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension. It is conjectured that the converse holds true in any dimension, but so far, the conjecture has been only established in the case of surfaces by Keel and McKernan [8].

It follows in particular from these results that for smooth affine surfaces the notions of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness and 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruledness coincide. Pursuing further the analogy with the classical projective notions, it seems then natural to expect that these do no longer coincide for higher dimensional affine varieties. Our main result confirms that this is indeed the case. Namely, we establish the following:

Theorem.

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the complement of a smooth hypersurface QnQ_{n} of degree nn in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled but not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled.

The anti-ampleness of the divisor Kℙn+QnK_{\mathbb{P}^{n}}+Q_{n} enables to easily deduce the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruledness of affine varieties of the form ℙn∖Qn\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus Q_{n} from the general log-deformation theory for rational curves developed by Keel and McKernan [8]. The failure of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness is then obtained in a more indirect fashion. Indeed, it turns out that for the varieties under consideration, 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness is equivalent to the stronger property that they admit a non trivial action of the additive group 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}. We then exploit two deep results of projective geometry, namely the non rationality of the smooth cubic threefold in ℙ4\mathbb{P}^{4} in the case n=3n=3 and the birational super-rigidity of smooth hypersurfaces Qn⊂ℙnQ_{n}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} if n≥4n\geq 4, to exclude the existence of such non trivial actions.

In the last section, we consider more closely the case of complements of smooth cubic surfaces in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} which provides a good illustration of the subtle but crucial difference between the two notions of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness and 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruledness in higher dimension. We show in particular that even though such complements are not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled they admit natural fibrations by 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces. We study automorphisms of such fibrations in relation with the problem of deciding whether every automorphism of the complement of a smooth cubic surface is induced by a linear transformation of the ambient space ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}.

1. Recollection on affine ruled and affine uniruled varieties

1.1. Affine ruledness and algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions

Here we review general properties of affine ruled varieties, with a particular focus on the interplay between 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness of an affine variety and the existence of non trivial algebraic actions of the additive group 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} on it. We refer the reader to [4] for basic properties of the correspondence between such actions on affine varieties and their algebraic counterpart, the so-called locally nilpotent derivations of their coordinate rings.

Definition 1.

A quasi-projective variety XX is called affine ruled or 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled if it contains a Zariski dense open subset UU of the form U≃𝔸1×YU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y for a suitable quasi-projective variety YY. An open subset of this type is called an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset of XX.

1.1.1.

An 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled variety XX is in particular ruled in the usual sense, the inclusion 𝔸1×Y↪X\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y\hookrightarrow X of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset of XX inducing a dominant birational map ℙ1×Y⇢X\mathbb{P}^{1}\times Y\dashrightarrow X. The converse is not true since for instance the product of the punctured affine line 𝔸∗1=𝔸1∖{0}\mathbb{A}_{*}^{1}=\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\} with a smooth projective curve of positive genus is ruled but does not contain any 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinder. In particular, in contrast with ruledness, the property of being 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled is not invariant under birational equivalence. Note similarly that the existence of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset of XX is a stronger requirement than that of a dominant birational morphism 𝔸1×Y→X\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y\rightarrow X for a suitable variety YY: for instance, the affine cone X⊆𝔸3X\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{3} over a projective plane curve C⊆ℙ2C\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{2} of positive genus does not contain 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders but on the other hand, blowing-up the vertex of the cone XX yields a smooth quasi-projective variety σ:X~→X\sigma:\tilde{X}\rightarrow X with the structure of a locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:X~→C\rho:\tilde{X}\rightarrow C hence, restricting to a subset YY of CC over which ρ\rho is trivial, a dominant birational morphism σ∣ρ−1​(Y):ρ−1​(Y)≃𝔸1×Y→X\sigma\mid_{{\rho^{-1}}(Y)}:\rho^{-1}(Y)\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y\rightarrow X.

1.1.2.

Typical examples of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled varieties are normal affine varieties X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) admitting a nontrivial algebraic action of the additive group 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}. Indeed, if XX is equipped with such an action induced by a locally nilpotent ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivation ∂\partial of AA, then for every local slice f∈Ker∂2∖Ker∂f\in\mathrm{Ker}\partial^{2}\setminus\mathrm{Ker}\partial, the principal open subset X∂f=Spec⁡(A∂f)X_{\partial f}=\mathrm{Spec}(A_{\partial f}), where A∂fA_{\partial f} denotes the localization A⁡[(∂f)−1]A[(\partial f)^{-1}] of AA, is 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-invariant and the morphism 𝔾a×(V⁡(f)∩X∂f)→X∂f\mathbb{G}_{a}\times(V(f)\cap X_{\partial f})\rightarrow X_{\partial f} induced by the 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX is an isomorphism. In particular, X∂fX_{\partial_{f}} is a principal 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset of XX. Note on the contrary that the existence of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset U≃𝔸1×YU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y of an affine variety X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) is in general not enough to guarantee that XX can be equipped with a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action whose general orbits coincide with the general fibers of the projection prY:U≃𝔸1×Y→Y\mathrm{pr}_{Y}:U\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y\rightarrow Y. For instance, the general fibers of the projection pr1:X=ℙ1×ℙ1∖Δ→ℙ1\mathrm{pr}_{1}:X=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\Delta\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, where Δ⊂ℙ1×ℙ1\Delta\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} denotes the diagonal, cannot coincides with general orbits of an algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX. Indeed, otherwise every invariant function on XX would descend to a regular function on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} and hence would be constant, in contradiction with the fact that for an affine variety XX, the field Frac⁡(Γ​(X,𝒪X)𝔾a)\mathrm{Frac}(\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})^{\mathbb{G}_{a}}) has transcendence degree dimX−1\dim X-1 over ℂ\mathbb{C}.

In fact, it is classically known that the general fibers of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical affine open subset U≃𝔸1×YU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y of a normal affine variety X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) coincide with the general orbits of an algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX if and only if UU is a principal affine open subset of XX (see e.g. [9, Proposition 3.1.5]). Let us briefly recall the argument for the convenience of the reader: the existence of a principal 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinder in XX is equivalent to the existence of an element a∈A∖{0}a\in A\setminus\left\{0\right\} and an isomorphism of ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra φ:Aa→∼B⁡[t]\varphi:A_{a}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}B[t], where tt is transcendental over Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac}(B). The derivation ∂0=φ∗∂∂t\partial_{0}=\varphi^{*}\frac{\partial}{\partial t} of AaA_{a} is then locally nilpotent and since AA is a finitely generated algebra, there exists n≥0n\geq 0 such that an∂0a^{n}\partial_{0} induces a ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivation ∂\partial of AA. Noting that being invertible in AaA_{a}, aa is necessarily contained in the kernel of ∂0\partial_{0}, we conclude that ∂\partial is a locally nilpotent derivation of AA, defining a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX whose restriction to the principal invariant open subset U=Spec⁡(Aa)≃Spec⁡(B)×𝔸1U={\rm Spec}(A_{a})\simeq\mathrm{Spec}(B)\times\mathbb{A}^{1} is by construction equivariantly isomorphic to that by translations on the second factor.

It follows in particular that for a normal affine variety XX whose divisor class group Cl⁡(X)\mathrm{Cl}(X) is torsion, the existence of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subsets is essentially equivalent to that of nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions. More precisely, we have the following criterion:

Proposition 2.

Let X=Spec⁡(A)X=\mathrm{Spec}(A) be a normal affine variety such that Cl⁡(X)⊗ℤℚ=0\mathrm{Cl}(X)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}=0. Then for every 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset U≃𝔸1×YU\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y of XX there exists an action of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} on XX whose general orbits coincide with the general fibers of the projection prY:U→Y\mathrm{pr}_{Y}:U\rightarrow Y. In particular, XX admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinder open subset if and only if it admits a nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action.

Proof.

By replacing YY by an affine open subset of it, we may assume that UU is affine whence that its complement D=X∖UD=X\setminus U has pure codimension one in XX as XX itself is affine. The hypothesis guarantees precisely that DD is the support of a principal divisor and hence the assertions follow immediately from the discussion above. ∎

1.2. Basic facts on log uniruled quasi-projective varieties

Definition 3.

A quasi-projective variety XX is called 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled, or (properly) log-uniruled after [8] if it contains a Zariski dense open subset UU with the property that for every x∈Ux\in U, there exists a non constant morphism fx:𝔸1→Xf_{x}:\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X such that x∈fx​(𝔸1)x\in f_{x}(\mathbb{A}^{1}).

1.2.1.

Equivalently, XX is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled if through a general point there exists a maximally affine rational curve, that is, an affine rational curve whose normalization is isomorphic to the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. An 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled variety is in particular uniruled in the usual sense, i.e. there exists a dominant, generically finite rational map ℙ1×Y⇢X\mathbb{P}^{1}\times Y\dashrightarrow X for a suitable quasi-projective variety YY. More precisely, letting (V,D)(V,D) be a pair consisting of a projective model VV of XX and a, possibly empty, boundary divisor DD such that VV is smooth along DD, it follows from [8, 5.1] that there exists a closed sub-scheme YY of Mor⁡(ℙ1,V)\mathrm{Mor}(\mathbb{P}^{1},V) consisting of morphisms f:ℙ1→Vf:\mathbb{P}^{1}\rightarrow V with the property that f−1​(f⁡(ℙ1)∩D)f^{-1}(f(\mathbb{P}^{1})\cap D) consists of at most one point and on which the restriction of the canonical evaluation morphism ev:ℙ1×Mor⁡(ℙ1,V)→V\mathrm{ev}:\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathrm{Mor}(\mathbb{P}^{1},V)\rightarrow V induces a dominant morphism ℙ1×Y→V\mathbb{P}^{1}\times Y\rightarrow V.

1.2.2.

It is not difficult to check that a smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled quasi-projective variety XX has logarithmic Kodaira dimension κ¯​(X)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(X)=-\infty (see e.g. [8, 5.11]). The converse holds true in dimension ≤2\leq 2 thanks to the successive works of Miyanishi-Sugie [14] and Keel-McKernan [8] and in fact, for a smooth affine surface XX, the three conditions κ¯​(X)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(X)=-\infty, XX is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled and XX is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled turn out to be equivalent to each other. Furthermore, the surface XX has then the stronger property that every of its point belongs to a maximally affine rational curve. This follows from the fact that the projection prY:U≃𝔸1×Y→Y\mathrm{pr}_{Y}:U\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times Y\rightarrow Y from an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylindrical open subset UU extends to a fibration p:X→Zp:X\rightarrow Z over an open subset of a smooth projective model of YY, with general fibers isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} and whose degenerate fibers consist of disjoint unions of affine lines (see e.g. [13]). Meanwhile, much less is known in higher dimension where one lacks in particular a good logarithmic analogue of Mori’s Bend-and-Break techniques. Nevertheless, the following simple criterion due to Keel and McKernan [8, Corollary 5.4] enables to easily confirm 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness of certain smooth affine varieties and will be enough for our purpose:

Theorem 4.

Let XX be a smooth affine variety and let X↪(V,D)X\hookrightarrow(V,D) be a projective completion where VV is a smooth projective variety and D=V∖XD=V\setminus X a reduced divisor on VV. If −(KV+D)-(K_{V}+D) is ample then XX is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled.

Example 5.

The above criterion guarantees for instance that for every n≥1n\geq 1, the complement XX of a hypersurface D⊆ℙnD\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n} of degree d≤nd\leq n is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled. In dimension 22, we recover in particular the fact that the complement of smooth conic Q2Q_{2} in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled, actually 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled say for instance by the restriction to ℙ2∖Q2\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus Q_{2} of the rational pencil generated by Q2Q_{2} and two times its tangent line at a given point. On the other hand, even though the criterion does not require DD to be an SNC divisor, it does not enable to deduce the fact that the complement of a cuspidal cubic DD is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled, in fact again 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled, namely via the restriction of the rational pencil on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} generated by DD and three times its tangent line at the singular point.

2. Complement of smooth hypersurfaces of degree nn in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, n≥3n\geq 3

According to Theorem 4, the complement XX of a hypersurface QnQ_{n} of degree nn in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, is a smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled affine variety. If n=2n=2, then Q2Q_{2} is a smooth conic whose complement is in fact 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled (see Example 5). Here we show in contrast that for every n≥3n\geq 3, the complement of a smooth hypersurface Qn⊆ℙnQ_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n} is not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled. It is worthwhile to note that the strategy to establish this fact in case of n=3n=3 is quite different from that of the case of n≥4n\geq 4.

2.1. The case n≥4n\geq 4

Here we will exploit the birational super-rigidity of smooth hypersurfaces Qn⊂ℙnQ_{n}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} of degree n≥4n\geq 4 to deduce that the corresponding affine varieties X=ℙn∖QnX=\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus Q_{n} are not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled. Let us first briefly recall the notion of birational super-rigidity for a class of variety which is enough for our needs (see e.g. [17] for the general definition).

Definition 6.

A smooth Fano variety VV with Pic⁡(V)≃ℤ\mathrm{Pic}(V)\simeq\mathbb{Z} is called birationaly super-rigid if the following two conditions hold:

a) The variety VV is not birational to a fibration V′→SV^{\prime}\rightarrow S onto a variety of dim​S>0{\rm dim}S>0 whose general fibers are smooth varieties with Kodaira dimension −∞-\infty,

b) Any birational map from VV to another smooth Fano variety V′V^{\prime} with Pic⁡(V′)≃ℤ\mathrm{Pic}(V^{\prime})\simeq\mathbb{Z} is a biregular isomorphism.

The essential ingredient we will use is the following result, first established by Pukhlikov [17] under suitable generality assumptions and recently extended to arbitrary smooth hypersurfaces by De Fernex [3]:

Theorem 7.

Let n≥4n\geq 4 and let Qn⊆ℙnQ_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n} be a smooth hypersurface of degree nn. Then QnQ_{n} is birationaly super-rigid.

Remark 8.

A noteworthy consequence of the above result is that every birational map Qn⇢Qn′⊂ℙnQ_{n}\dashrightarrow Q_{n}^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} between smooth hypersurfaces of degree nn is in fact a biregular isomorphism which has the additional property to be induced by the restriction of a linear transformation of the ambient space ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. This follows from the fact that anti-canonical divisors on QnQ_{n} coincide with hyperplane sections of QnQ_{n}. In particular, the group Bir⁡(Qn)\mathrm{Bir}(Q_{n}) of birational automorphisms of QnQ_{n} coincides with that of projective automorphisms Lin⁡(Qn)\mathrm{Lin}(Q_{n}) and the latter is a finite group.

Now we are ready to prove the following:

Proposition 9.

The complement of every smooth hypersurface Qn⊆ℙnQ_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n} of degree n≥4n\geq 4 is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled but not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled.

Proof.

The 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruledness of X=ℙn∖QnX=\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus Q_{n} is an immediate consequence of Theorem 4. Since Cl⁡(X)=ℤ/n​ℤ\mathrm{Cl}(X)=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, it follows from Proposition 2 that the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness of XX is equivalent to the existence of a non trivial algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on it. Every given 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX induces a one parameter family of automorphisms {φt}t∈𝔾a\{\varphi_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{G}_{a}} of XX that we interpret through the open inclusion X=ℙn∖Qn↪ℙnX=\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus Q_{n}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n} as birational automorphisms Φt:ℙn⇢ℙn\Phi_{t}:\mathbb{P}^{n}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n}, t∈𝔾at\in\mathbb{G}_{a}. Since QnQ_{n} is birationally super-rigid by virtue of Theorem 7 above, it follows that every Φt\Phi_{t} is in fact a biregular automorphism. Indeed, otherwise, noting that Φt\Phi_{t} cannot be an isomorphism in codimension one (see e.g. [2]) and letting ℙn←pV→qℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\leftarrow}}V\stackrel{{\scriptstyle q}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathbb{P}^{n} be a resolution of it, where pp consists of successive blow-ups of smooth centers, it would follow that the proper transform q∗−1​Qnq_{*}^{-1}Q_{n} of QnQ_{n} in VV is an exceptional divisor of pp whence is birationally ruled in contradiction with condition a) in Definition 6. Therefore the 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX extends to a linear one on ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} which leaves XX whence QnQ_{n} invariant. Since the automorphism group Aut⁡(Qn)\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{n}) is finite (see Remark 8 above), the induced 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on QnQ_{n} is the trivial one and so, being linear, the 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} extending that on XX is trivial on the linear span of QnQ_{n}. But QnQ_{n} is obviously not contained in any hyperplane of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} and hence the initial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XX is necessarily trivial, which completes the proof. ∎

2.2. The case n=3n=3: complements of smooth cubic surfaces in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}

Since a smooth cubic surface Q3Q_{3} in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} is rational, the same argument as in the previous section depending on birational super-rigidity is no longer applicable to deduce the non 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness of its complement X=ℙ3∖Q3X=\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q_{3}. Instead, we will derive it from the unirationality but non rationality of smooth cubic threefolds in ℙ4\mathbb{P}^{4} together with a suitable finite étale covering trick.

The divisor class group of the complement XX of a smooth cubic surface Q3⊆ℙ3Q_{3}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3} being isomorphic to ℤ/3​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z} generated by the class of a hyperplane section, it follows again from Proposition 2 that XX is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled if and only if it admits a non trivial algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action. On the other hand, since algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions lift under finite étale covers (see e.g. [18]), to establish the non 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness of XX it is enough to exhibit a finite étale cover π:X~→X\pi:\tilde{X}\rightarrow X of XX with the property that X~\tilde{X} does not admit any non trivial algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action.

Proposition 10.

Let X=ℙ3∖Q3X=\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q_{3} be the complement of a smooth cubic surface and let π:X~→X\pi:\tilde{X}\rightarrow X be the canonical étale Galois cover of degree three associated with the canonical sheaf ωX≃𝒪ℙ1​(−1)∣X\omega_{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)\mid_{X} of XX. Then X~\tilde{X} is a smooth affine threefold which does not admit any non trivial algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action. Consequently, XX is not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled.

Proof.

Letting Q3⊆ℙ3=Proj⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z,u])Q_{3}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3}=\mathrm{Proj}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,u]) be defined as the zero locus of a homogeneous polynomial F⁡(x,y,z,u)∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z,u]F(x,y,z,u)\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,u] of degree three, it is straightforward to check that the canonical triple étale covering X~\tilde{X} of XX is isomorphic to the affine variety 𝔸4=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z,u])\mathbb{A}^{4}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,u]) defined by the equation F⁡(x,y,z,u)=1F(x,y,z,u)=1, and that the morphism π:X~→X\pi:\tilde{X}\rightarrow X coincides with the restriction of the natural morphism 𝔸4∖{0}→ℙ3\mathbb{A}^{4}\setminus\left\{0\right\}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{3}, (x,y,z,u)↦[x:y:z:u](x,y,z,u)\mapsto[x:y:z:u]. Note that by construction, X~\tilde{X} is an open subset of the smooth cubic threefold V⊆Proj⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z,u,v])V\subseteq\mathrm{Proj}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,u,v]) with equation F⁡(x,y,z,u)−v3=0F(x,y,z,u)-v^{3}=0, hence is unirational but not rational by virtue of a famous result of Clemens-Griffiths [1]. Now suppose that there exists a non trivial algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on X~\tilde{X}. Then by virtue of [19], the algebra of invariants Γ​(X~,𝒪X~)𝔾a\Gamma(\tilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{X}})^{\mathbb{G}_{a}} is a finitely generated integrally closed domain of transcendence degree two over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Letting q:X~→Z~=Spec⁡(Γ​(X~,𝒪X~)𝔾a)q:\tilde{X}\rightarrow\tilde{Z}=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(\tilde{X},\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{X}})^{\mathbb{G}_{a}}) be the corresponding quotient morphism, the unirationality of X~\tilde{X} implies that of Z~\tilde{Z} whence its rationality since these two notions coincide in dimension two. But then the existence of a principal affine open subset Z~a\tilde{Z}_{a} of Z~\tilde{Z} such that q−1​(Z~a)≃𝔸1×Z~aq^{-1}(\tilde{Z}_{a})\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\tilde{Z}_{a} (see §\lx@sectionsign 1.1.2 above) would imply in turn that X~\tilde{X} itself is rational, a contradiction.∎

Remark 11.

Complements of singular cubic surfaces Q3⊆ℙ3Q_{3}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3} may turn out to be 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled. For instance, it is shown in [10] that if Q3Q_{3} has Du Val singularities worse than A2A_{2} then ℙ3∖Q3\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q_{3} admits a non trivial algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action. It may even happen that ℙ3∖Q3\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q_{3} contains an 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinder, i.e., an open subset of the form 𝔸2×Y\mathbb{A}^{2}\times Y for a smooth curve YY. This holds for instance for the complement of the cubic surface Q⊆ℙ3=Proj⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z,u])Q\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3}=\mathrm{Proj}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,u]) defined as the vanishing locus of the homogeneous polynomial F⁡(x,y,z,u)=y​u2+z⁡(x​z+y2)F(x,y,z,u)=yu^{2}+z(xz+y^{2}) which has a unique isolated singularity [1:0:0:0]\left[1:0:0:0\right] of type D5D_{5}. Indeed, noting that f⁡(x,y,z)=F⁡(x,y,z,1)f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z,1) is a component of the Nagata automorphism [15], it follows that the general fibers of the morphism ρ:ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho:\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} induced by the restriction of the rational pencil on ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} generated by QQ and three times the hyperplane {u=0}\{u=0\} are isomorphic to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} hence, by virtue of [7], that there exists an open subset Y⊆𝔸1Y\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{1} such that ρ−1​(Y)≃𝔸2×Y\rho^{-1}(Y)\simeq\mathbb{A}^{2}\times Y. A similar construction holds for all normal cubic surfaces listed in [16] which arise as closures in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} of zero sets of components of automorphisms of 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}.

3. Rigid rational fibrations on complements of smooth cubic surfaces in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}

In contrast with the higher dimensional case where a similar argument as the one used in the proof of Proposition 9 shows that for every smooth hypersurface QnQ_{n} of the degree nn in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, n≥4n\geq 4, the group Aut⁡(ℙn∖Qn)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus Q_{n}) is embeded as a subgroup of Aut⁡(Qn)\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{n}) hence consists of a finite group of linear transformations, it is not known whether every automorphism of the complement of a smooth cubic surface Q=Q3Q=Q_{3} in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} is induced by a linear transformation of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}.

Even though ℙ3\Q{\mathbb{P}}^{3}\backslash Q is not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled (cf. Proposition 10), it turns out that it is fibered in a natural way by 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces whose general closures in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} are smooth cubic surfaces. Since 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces are usually good candidates for having non trivial automorphisms, one can expect that these fibrations have interesting automorphisms, in particular automorphisms induced by strictly birational transformations of the ambient space ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}.

In this section, we first review the construction of these fibrations ρ:ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho:\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} by 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces. We describe the automorphism groups of their general fibers and we check in particular that for a general smooth cubic hypersurface Q⊆ℙ3Q\subseteq{\mathbb{P}}^{3}, these fibers do indeed carry interesting automorphisms induced by strictly birational Geiser involutions of their projective closures. We show in contrast that every automorphism of the full fibration comes as the restriction of a linear transformation of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}.

3.1. Special rational pencils on the complement of a smooth cubic surface

Given a smooth cubic surface Q⊆ℙ3Q\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3} and a line LL on it, the restriction to QQ of the rational pencil ℋL=|𝒪ℙ3​(1)⊗ℐL|\mathcal{H}_{L}=\left|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{3}}(1)\otimes\mathcal{I}_{L}\right| on ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} generated by planes containing LL can be decomposed as ℋL∣Q=ℒ+L\mathcal{H}_{L}\mid_{Q}=\mathcal{L}+L where ℒ\mathcal{L} is a base point free pencil defining a conic bundle Φℒ:Q→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}:Q\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with five degenerate fibers, each consisting of the union of two (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves intersecting transversally. The restriction Φℒ∣L:L→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}\mid_{L}:L\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is a double cover and for every branch point x∈ℙ1x\in\mathbb{P}^{1} of Φℒ∣L\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}\mid_{L}, the intersection of QQ with the corresponding hyperplane Hx∈ℋLH_{x}\in\mathcal{H}_{L} consists either of a smooth conic tangent to LL or of two distinct lines intersecting LL in a same point, which is called an Eckardt point of QQ. Letting say H0​(L)H_{0}(L) and H∞​(L)H_{\infty}(L) be the planes in ℋL\mathcal{H}_{L} such that Φℒ∣L\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}\mid_{L} is ramified over the points Φℒ​(Ht​(L)∣Q−L)\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}(H_{t}(L)\mid_{Q}-L), t=0,∞t=0,\infty, the divisors QQ and 3​Ht​(L)3H_{t}(L) generate a pencil of cubic surfaces ρ¯t​(L):ℙ3⇢ℙ1\overline{\rho}_{t}(L):\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with a unique multiple member 3​Ht​(L)3H_{t}(L) and whose general members are smooth cubic surfaces.

3.1.1.

From now on we consider a pencil ρ¯=ρ¯t​(L)\overline{\rho}=\overline{\rho}_{t}(L) as above associated to a fixed line L⊆QL\subseteq Q and a fixed distinguished plane H∈ℋLH\in\mathcal{H}_{L} intersecting QQ either along the union L∪CL\cup C of a line and conic intersecting each other in a single point pp or along the union L∪L1∪L2L\cup L_{1}\cup L_{2} of three lines meeting at an Eckardt point pp of QQ. We denote by ρ:ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho:\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} the morphism induced by the restriction of ρ¯\overline{\rho} to the complement of QQ. By construction, the closure in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} of a general fiber SS of ρ\rho is a smooth cubic surface VV such that the reduced divisor D=H∩VD=H\cap V has either the form D=L+CD=L+C or D=L+L1+L2D=L+L_{1}+L_{2}. In each case we denote by α:W→V\alpha:W\rightarrow V the blow-up of pp, with exceptional divisor EE. If pp is an Eckardt point, then we let V~=W\tilde{V}=W and we denote by D~⊆V~\tilde{D}\subseteq\tilde{V} the reduced divisor α−1​(D)red=L+L1+L2+E\alpha^{-1}(D)_{\mathrm{red}}=L+L_{1}+L_{2}+E. Otherwise, if pp is not an Eckardt point, then we let V~\tilde{V} be the variety obtained from WW by blowing-up further the intersection point of EE and of the proper transform of CC, say with exceptional divisor E2E_{2}, and we let D~⊆V~\tilde{D}\subseteq\tilde{V} be the reduced divisor D~=L+C+E+E2\tilde{D}=L+C+E+E_{2}. By construction, D~\tilde{D} is an SNC divisor and the induced birational morphism σ:(V~,D~)→(V,D)\sigma:(\tilde{V},\tilde{D})\rightarrow(V,D) provides a minimal log-resolution of the pair (V,D)\left(V,D\right).

The following lemma summarizes basic properties of the general fibers of fibrations of the form ρt​(L):ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho_{t}(L):\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}, t=0,∞t=0,\infty.

Lemma 12.

For a general fiber S=V∖DS=V\setminus D of ρt​(L):ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho_{t}(L):\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}, the following holds:

a) SS is a smooth affine surface with a trivial canonical sheaf and logarithmic Kodaira dimension κ¯​(S)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(S)=-\infty,

b) If D=L+CD=L+C (resp. D=L+L1+L2D=L+L_{1}+L_{2}) then the Picard group of SS is isomorphic to ℤ5\mathbb{Z}^{5} (resp. ℤ4\mathbb{Z}^{4}).

Proof.

The affineness of SS is clear as DD is a hyperplane section of VV. Since VV is a smooth cubic surface, it follows from adjunction formula that ωV≃ωℙ3⊗𝒪ℙ3​(3)∣V≃𝒪ℙ3​(−1)∣V≃𝒪V​(−D)\omega_{V}\simeq\omega_{\mathbb{P}^{3}}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{3}}(3)\mid_{V}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{3}}(-1)\mid_{V}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{V}(-D). This implies in turn the triviality of the canonical sheaf of SS as ωS≃ωV∣S≃𝒪V​(−D)∣S≃𝒪S\omega_{S}\simeq\omega_{V}\mid_{S}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{V}(-D)\mid_{S}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{S}. We may identify SS with V~∖D~\tilde{V}\setminus\tilde{D} via the birational morphism σ:(V~,D~)→(V,D)\sigma:(\tilde{V},\tilde{D})\rightarrow(V,D) constructed above. Since D~\tilde{D} is an SNC divisor by construction, we have κ¯​(S)=κ⁡(V~,KV~+D~)\overline{\kappa}(S)=\kappa(\tilde{V},K_{\tilde{V}}+\tilde{D}). Using the fact that −D-D is a canonical divisor on VV, we deduce from the logarithmic ramification formula for σ\sigma that

{KV~+D~=−Eif ​D=L+L1+L2KV~+D~=−E2if ​D=L+C.\begin{cases}K_{\tilde{V}}+\tilde{D}=-E&\textrm{if }D=L+L_{1}+L_{2}\\ K_{\tilde{V}}+\tilde{D}=-E_{2}&\textrm{if }D=L+C.\end{cases}

Since EE and E2E_{2} are exceptional divisors, one has H0​(V~,m⁡(KV~+D~))=0H^{0}(\tilde{V},m(K_{\tilde{V}}+\tilde{D}))=0 for every m>0m>0 and hence κ¯​(S)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(S)=-\infty.

To determine the Picard group of SS, we will exploit the conic bundle structure Φℒ:V→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} described in the beginning of 3.1. By contracting a suitable irreducible component of each of the five degenerate fibers of Φℒ:V→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, we obtain a birational morphism τ:V→ℙ1×ℙ1\tau:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} fitting into a commutative diagram

V\displaystyle V →τ\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tau}}{{\rightarrow}} ℙ1×ℙ1\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}
Φℒ↓\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}\downarrow ↓pr1\displaystyle\downarrow\mathrm{pr}_{1}
ℙ1\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{1} =\displaystyle= ℙ1\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{1}

and such that the proper transform of LL is a smooth 22-section of pr1\mathrm{pr}_{1} with self-intersection 44, whence a section of the second projection pr2:ℙ1×ℙ1→ℙ1\mathrm{pr}_{2}:\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}. We can then identify the divisor class group Cl⁡(V)≃ℤ7\mathrm{Cl}(V)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{7} of VV with the group generated by the proper transforms of a fiber of pr1\mathrm{pr_{1}}, a fiber of pr2\mathrm{pr}_{2}, and the five exceptional divisors of τ\tau. The proper transform τ∗​(D)\tau_{*}(D) of DD in ℙ1×ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} is the union of the proper transform of LL and of a fiber of pr1\mathrm{pr}_{1}. Thus if D=L+CD=L+C then LL and CC together with the five exceptional divisors of τ\tau generate Cl⁡(V)\mathrm{Cl}(V) and hence Cl⁡(S)≃Pic⁡(S)\mathrm{Cl}(S)\simeq\mathrm{Pic}(S) is isomorphic to ℤ5\mathbb{Z}^{5} generated by the classes of the intersections of these exceptional divisors with SS. Similarly, if D=L+L1+L2D=L+L_{1}+L_{2} then L1L_{1} or L2L_{2}, say L2L_{2}, is an exceptional divisor of τ\tau and so Cl⁡(V)\mathrm{Cl}(V) is generated by LL, L1L_{1}, L2L_{2} and the four other exceptional divisors of τ\tau. This implies in turn that Cl⁡(S)≃Pic⁡(S)\mathrm{Cl}(S)\simeq\mathrm{Pic}(S) is isomorphic to ℤ4\mathbb{Z}^{4} generated by the classes of the intersections of these four exceptional divisors with SS. ∎

3.1.2.

Since a general fiber S=V∖DS=V\setminus D of ρt​(L):ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho_{t}(L):\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} has logarithmic Kodaira dimension −∞-\infty by Lemma 12, it is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled and hence, by virtue of [13], it admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→Cq:S\rightarrow C over a smooth curve. Let us briefly explain how to construct such fibrations using the birational morphism τ:V→ℙ1×ℙ1\tau:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} which contracts an irreducible component of each of the five degenerate fibers of Φℒ:V→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} as described in the proof of the previous Lemma. According to the configuration of DD, we have the following:

a) If D=L+CD=L+C where CC is a smooth conic, then each of the points blown-up by τ\tau is the intersection point of the proper transform of LL with a fiber of pr2:ℙ1×ℙ1→ℙ1\mathrm{pr}_{2}:\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}. The proper transforms F1,…,F5⊆VF_{1},\ldots,F_{5}\subseteq V of these fibers are disjoint (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves which do not intersect LL. Let μ:V→ℙ2\mu:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} be the contraction of LL and F1,…,F5F_{1},\ldots,F_{5}. Since each FiF_{i}, i=1,…,5i=1,\ldots,5 intersects CC transversally and LL is tangent to CC, the image of CC in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is a cuspidal cubic. The rational pencil on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} generated by the image of CC and three times its tangent line TT at its unique singular point lifts to a rational pencil q¯:V⇢ℙ1\overline{q}:V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} having the divisors C+∑i=15FiC+\sum_{i=1}^{5}F_{i} and 3​T+L3T+L as singular members. Its restriction to S=V∖DS=V\setminus D is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→ℙ1q:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers: one is irreducible of multiplicity three consisting of the intersection of the proper transform of TT with SS and the other is reduced, consisting of the disjoint union of the curves Fi∩S≃𝔸1F_{i}\cap S\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,5i=1,\ldots,5.

b) The construction in the case where D=L+L1+L2D=L+L_{1}+L_{2} is very similar: we may suppose that L1L_{1} is contracted by τ\tau so that contracting the same irreducible components F1,…,F4F_{1},\ldots,F_{4} of the degenerate fibers of Φℒ:V→ℙ1\Phi_{\mathcal{L}}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} but L2L_{2} instead of L1L_{1}, we obtain a birational morphism τ1:V→𝔽1\tau_{1}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{1}. The image of LL in 𝔽1\mathbb{F}_{1} is a smooth 22-section of the ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle structure π1:𝔽1→ℙ1\pi_{1}:\mathbb{F}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with self-intersection 44. Letting C0C_{0} be the exceptional section of π1\pi_{1} with self-intersection (−1)\left(-1\right), one has necessarily L∼2​C0+2​FL\sim 2C_{0}+2F where FF is a fiber of π1\pi_{1}. So LL does not intersect C0C_{0} and its image in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} by the morphism q:𝔽1→ℙ2q:\mathbb{F}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} contracting C0C_{0} is a smooth conic. Since L1L_{1} is tangent to LL in 𝔽1\mathbb{F}_{1}, its image in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is the tangent to the image of CC at a point distinct from the one blown-up by qq. The rational pencil on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} generated by the image of LL and two times that of L1L_{1} lifts to a rational pencil ρ¯:V⇢ℙ1\overline{\rho}:V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} having 2​L1+L2+2​C02L_{1}+L_{2}+2C_{0} and L+∑i=14FiL+\sum_{i=1}^{4}F_{i} as degenerate members. Its restriction to S=V∖DS=V\setminus D yields an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:S→ℙ1\rho:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers : one is irreducible of multiplicity two consisting of the intersection of the proper transform of C0C_{0} with SS and the other is reduced, consisting of the disjoint union of the curves Fi∩S≃𝔸1F_{i}\cap S\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4.

Remark 13.

It follows from Corollary 15 below that the automorphism group of a smooth affine surface S=V∖DS=V\setminus D as above is finite. In particular, such surfaces are 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled but do not admit non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions and so the complement of a smooth cubic surface Q⊆ℙ3Q\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3} is a smooth affine 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled threefold without non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action which has the structure of a family ρt​(L):ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho_{t}(L):\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces without non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions. In contrast, the total space of a family of affine varieties with non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions often admits itself a non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action. For instance, suppose that φ:X=Spec⁡(B)→S=Spec⁡(A)\varphi:X=\mathrm{Spec}(B)\rightarrow S=\mathrm{Spec}(A) is a dominant morphism between complex affine varieties and that ∂:B→B\partial:B\rightarrow B is an AA-derivation of BB which is locally nilpotent in restriction to general closed fibers of φ\varphi, defining non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on these fibers. Then ∂\partial is a locally nilpotent AA-derivation of BB and hence XX carries a non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action. Indeed, up to shrinking SS if necessary, we may assume that for every maximal ideal 𝔪∈Specmax⁡(A)\mathfrak{m}\in\mathrm{Specmax}(A), the A/𝔪A/\mathfrak{m}-derivation ∂𝔪:B/𝔪​B→B/𝔪​B\partial_{\mathfrak{m}}:B/\mathfrak{m}B\rightarrow B/\mathfrak{m}B induced by ∂\partial is locally nilpotent. Given an element f∈Bf\in B and an integer n≥0n\geq 0, denote by Kn​(f)K^{n}(f) the closed sub-variety of SS whose points are the maximal ideals 𝔪∈Specmax⁡(A)\mathfrak{m}\in\mathrm{\mathrm{Specmax}(A)} for which the residue class of ff in B/𝔪​BB/\mathfrak{m}B belongs to Ker∂𝔪n\mathrm{Ker}\partial_{\mathfrak{m}}^{n}. The hypothesis implies that SS is equal to the increasing union of its closed sub-variety Kn​(f)K^{n}(f), n≥0n\geq 0, and so this sequence must stabilizes as the base field ℂ\mathbb{C} is uncountable. So there exists n0=n0​(f)n_{0}=n_{0}(f) such that the restriction of ∂n0f\partial^{n_{0}}f to every closed fiber of φ:X→S\varphi:X\rightarrow S is the zero function, and hence ∂n0f=0\partial^{n_{0}}f=0 since these fibers form a dense subset of XX.

3.2. Automorphisms of general fibers of special rational pencils

This sub-section is devoted to the study of automorphisms of general fibers of the rational fibrations ρ:ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho:\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} constructed as above. We show in particular that such general fibers admit biregular involutions induced by Geiser involutions of their projective closures.

3.2.1.

To simplify the discussion, let us call a pair (V,D)\left(V,D\right) as in 3.1.1 special if VV is a smooth cubic hypersurface in ℙ3{\mathbb{P}}^{3} and DD is composed of three concurrent lines L+L1+L2L+L_{1}+L_{2} meeting in an Eckardt point pp of VV, or of the union of LL and a smooth conic CC intersecting LL with multiplicity two in a single point pp. Similarly as in §\lx@sectionsign 3.1.1, we denote by α:W→V\alpha:W\rightarrow V the blow-up of pp and we denote by EE its exceptional divisor.

By construction, WW is a weak del Pezzo surface (i.e., −KW-K_{W} is nef and big) of degree 22 on which the anticanonical linear system |−KW||-K_{W}| defines a morphism θ:W→ℙ2\theta:W\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2}. The latter factors into a birational morphism W→YW\rightarrow Y contracting LL (resp. LL, L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}) if D=L+CD=L+C (resp. if OPEND=L+L1+L2)D=L+L_{1}+L_{2}) followed by a Galois double covering Y→ℙ2Y\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} ramified over a quartic curve Δ\Delta with a unique double point (resp. three double points) located at the image of LL (resp. at the images of LL, L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}). The non trivial involution of the double covering Y→ℙ2Y\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} induces an involution GW:W→WG_{W}:W\rightarrow W fixing LL and exchanging the proper transform of DD and the exceptional divisor EE (resp. fixing LL, L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}). The latter descends either to birational involution GV,p:V⇢VG_{V,p}:V\dashrightarrow V if D=L+CD=L+C, or to a biregular involution GV,p:V→VG_{V,p}:V\rightarrow V having pp as an isolated fixed point if D=L+L1+L2D=L+L_{1}+L_{2}.

In each case, we say that GV,pG_{V,p} is the Geiser involution of VV with center at pp. By construction, GV,pG_{V,p} restricts further to a biregular involution jGV,pj_{G_{V,p}} of the affine surface S=V∖DS=V\setminus D which we call the affine Geiser involution of SS with center at pp.

Proposition 14.

Let φ:S=V∖D→∼S′=V′∖D′\varphi:S=V\setminus D\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}S^{\prime}=V^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime} be an isomorphism between affine surfaces associated to special pairs (V,D)\left(V,D\right) and (V′,D′)\left(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}\right) respectively. Then the following assertions hold:

a) If either DD or D′D^{\prime} consists of three concurrent lines then φ\varphi extends to an isomorphism of pairs φ¯:(V,D)→∼(V′,D′)\overline{\varphi}:\left(V,D\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}).

b) Otherwise, if both D=L+CD=L+C and D′=L′+C′D^{\prime}=L^{\prime}+C^{\prime} consist of the union of a line and a conic, then the induced birational map φ¯:V⇢V′\overline{\varphi}:V\dashrightarrow V^{\prime} is either an isomorphism of pairs, or it can be decomposed as φ¯=Ψ∘GV,p\overline{\varphi}=\Psi\circ G_{V,p} or φ¯=GV′,p′∘Ψ′\overline{\varphi}=G_{V^{\prime},p^{\prime}}\circ\Psi^{\prime} where Ψ,Ψ′\Psi,\Psi^{\prime} are isomorphisms of pairs and where GV,pG_{V,p} and GV′,p′G_{V^{\prime},p^{\prime}} denote the Geiser involutions of VV and V′V^{\prime} with centers are p=L∩Cp=L\cap C and p′=L′∩C′p^{\prime}=L^{\prime}\cap C^{\prime} respectively. Furthermore, every birational map V⇢V′V\dashrightarrow V^{\prime} of the form Ψ∘GV,p\Psi\circ G_{V,p} (resp. GV′,p′∘Ψ′G_{V^{\prime},p^{\prime}}\circ\Psi^{\prime}) can be uniquely re-written in the form GV′,p′∘Ψ′G_{V^{\prime},p^{\prime}}\circ\Psi^{\prime} (resp. Ψ∘GV,p\Psi\circ G_{V,p}). In particular, if there exists an isomorphism φ:S=V∖D→∼S′=V′∖D′\varphi:S=V\setminus D\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}S^{\prime}=V^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime} then VV and V′V^{\prime} are isomorphic smooth cubic surfaces.

Proof.

Let σ:(V~,D~)→(V,D)\sigma:(\tilde{V},\tilde{D})\rightarrow(V,D) and σ′:(V~′,D~′)→(V′,D′)\sigma^{\prime}:(\tilde{V}^{\prime},\tilde{D}^{\prime})\rightarrow(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}) be the minimal log-resolutions of the pairs (V,D)\left(V,D\right) and (V′,D′)(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}) respectively described in §\lx@sectionsign 3.1.1. Since V∖D≃V~∖D~V\setminus D\simeq\tilde{V}\setminus\tilde{D} and V′∖D′≃V~′∖D~′V^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime}\simeq\tilde{V}^{\prime}\setminus\tilde{D}^{\prime} by construction, every isomorphism φ:S→S′\varphi:S\rightarrow S^{\prime} extends in a natural way to a birational map φ~:V~⇢V~′\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{V}\dashrightarrow\tilde{V}^{\prime} restricting to φ\varphi on SS. We claim that φ~\tilde{\varphi} is in fact a biregular isomorphism of pairs. Indeed, suppose on the contrary that φ~\tilde{\varphi} is strictly birational and let V~←βX→β′V~′\tilde{V}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta}}{{\leftarrow}}X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta^{\prime}}}{{\rightarrow}}\tilde{V}^{\prime} be its minimal resolution. Recall that the minimality of the resolution implies in particular that there is no (−1)\left(-1\right)-curve in XX which is exceptional for β\beta and β′\beta^{\prime} simultaneously. Since V~\tilde{V} is smooth and D~\tilde{D} is an SNC divisor, β′\beta^{\prime} decomposes into a finite sequence of blow-downs of successive (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves supported on the boundary B=β−1​(D~)red=(β′)−1​(D~)redB=\beta^{-1}(\tilde{D})_{\mathrm{red}}=(\beta^{\prime})^{-1}(\tilde{D})_{\mathrm{red}}. In view of the structure of D~\tilde{D}, the only possible (−1)\left(-1\right)-curve in BB which is not exceptional for β\beta is the proper transform of EE if D=L+L1+L2D=L+L_{1}+L_{2} or the proper transform of E2E_{2} if D=L+CD=L+C. But after the contraction of these curves, the boundary would no longer be an SNC divisor, a contradiction. This implies that φ~:V~→V~′\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{V}\rightarrow\tilde{V}^{\prime} is a morphism and the same argument shows that it does not contract any curve in the boundary D~\tilde{D}. So φ~:V~→V~′\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{V}\rightarrow\tilde{V}^{\prime} is an isomorphism restricting to an isomorphism between V~∖D~\tilde{V}\setminus\tilde{D} and V~′∖D~′\tilde{V}^{\prime}\setminus\tilde{D}^{\prime} whence an isomorphism between the pairs (V~,D~)(\tilde{V},\tilde{D}) and (V~′,D~′)(\tilde{V}^{\prime},\tilde{D}^{\prime}). It follows in particular that the intersection matrices of the divisors D~\tilde{D} and D~′\tilde{D}^{\prime} must be the same up to a permutation. In view of the description given in §\lx@sectionsign 3.1.1, we conclude that either DD and D′D^{\prime} simultaneously consist of three concurrent lines or of the union of a line and a smooth conic.

In the first case, since the exceptional divisors EE of the blow-up of VV at pp and E′E^{\prime} of the blow-up of V′V^{\prime} at p′p^{\prime} are the only (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves in D~\tilde{D} and D~′\tilde{D}^{\prime} respectively, the biregular isomorphism φ~:V~→V~′\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{V}\rightarrow\tilde{V}^{\prime} extending φ\varphi necessarily maps EE isomorphically onto E′E^{\prime}. So φ~\tilde{\varphi} descends to an isomorphism of pairs φ¯:(V,D)→(V′,D′)\overline{\varphi}:(V,D)\rightarrow(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}) which gives a).

In the second case, letting D=L+CD=L+C and D′=L′+C′D^{\prime}=L^{\prime}+C^{\prime}, a similar argument implies that the isomorphism φ~:V~→V~′\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{V}\rightarrow\tilde{V}^{\prime} maps E2E_{2} onto E2′E_{2}^{\prime} and the proper transform of LL onto that of L′L^{\prime}. This implies in turn that φ~\tilde{\varphi} descends to an isomorphism φ~1:W→W′\tilde{\varphi}_{1}:W\rightarrow W^{\prime} between the surfaces obtained from VV and V′V^{\prime} by blowing-up the points p=L∩Cp=L\cap C and p′=L′∩C′p^{\prime}=L^{\prime}\cap C^{\prime} with respective exceptional divisors EE and E′E^{\prime}. Now we have the following alternative: either φ~1\tilde{\varphi}_{1} maps EE and CC onto E′E^{\prime} and C′C^{\prime} respectively, and then it descends to a biregular isomorphism of pairs φ¯:(V,D)→(V′,D′)\overline{\varphi}:(V,D)\rightarrow(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}), or φ~1\tilde{\varphi}_{1} maps EE and CC onto C′C^{\prime} and E′E^{\prime} respectively. In the second case, by composing φ¯:V⇢V′\overline{\varphi}:V\dashrightarrow V^{\prime} either by GV,pG_{V,p} on the left or by GV′,p′G_{V^{\prime},p^{\prime}} on the right, we get a new birational maps Ψ,Ψ′:V⇢V′\Psi,\Psi^{\prime}:V\dashrightarrow V^{\prime} which lift to a birational map Ψ1:W⇢W′\Psi_{1}:W\dashrightarrow W^{\prime} mapping LL, EE and CC isomorphically onto L′L^{\prime}, E′E^{\prime} and C′C^{\prime} respectively. The last assertion about the uniqueness of the re-writing is clear by construction.∎

Corollary 15.

Let (V,D)(V,D) be a special pair and let S=V∖DS=V\setminus D be the corresponding affine surface. Then the following holds:

a) If DD consists of three concurrent lines then Aut⁡(S)\mathrm{Aut}(S) is a nontrivial finite subgroup of PGL⁡(4,ℂ)\mathrm{PGL}(4,\mathbb{C}) which coincides with the automorphism group Aut⁡(V,D)\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) of the pair (V,D)\left(V,D\right).

b) Otherwise, if DD consists of a line and a smooth conic, then we have an exact sequence

0→Aut⁡(V,D)→Aut⁡(S)→ℤ2⋅jGV,p→00\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(V,D)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(S)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cdot j_{G_{V,p}}\rightarrow 0

and an isomorphism Aut⁡(S)=Aut⁡(V,D)⋊ℤ2⋅jGV,p\mathrm{Aut}(S)=\mathrm{Aut}(V,D)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cdot j_{G_{V,p}}, where the affine Geiser involution jGV,pj_{G_{V,p}} acts on Aut⁡(V,D)\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) by jGV,p⋅Ψ=Ψ′j_{G_{V,p}}\cdot\Psi=\Psi^{\prime} where for every Ψ∈Aut⁡(V,D)\Psi\in\mathrm{Aut}(V,D), Ψ′\Psi^{\prime} is the unique automorphism of the pair (V,D)(V,D) such that Ψ∘GV,p=GV,p∘Ψ′\Psi\circ G_{V,p}=G_{V,p}\circ\Psi^{\prime}.

Proof.

Since V⊆ℙ3V\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3} is embedded by its anti-canonical linear system |−KV||-K_{V}|, every automorphism of VV is induced by a linear transformation of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. Furthermore, since DD is a hyperplane section of VV, Aut⁡(V,D)\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) is an algebraic sub-group of the group of linear transformation of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} preserving globally the corresponding hyperplane. The automorphism group of a smooth cubic surface in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} being finite, it follows that Aut⁡(V,D)\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) is a finite algebraic group. If DD consists of three concurrent lines, then their common point pp is an Eckardt point of VV which is always the isolated fixed point of a biregular involution of VV preserving DD. This shows that Aut⁡(V,D)\mathrm{Aut}(V,D) is never trivial in this case. In case b), where D=L+CD=L+C is the union of a line and smooth conic, the assertion is an immediate consequence of the previous Proposition 14. ∎

Remark 16.

If D=L+CD=L+C then every automorphism Ψ\Psi of the pair (V,D)\left(V,D\right) preserves the rational pencil q¯:V⇢ℙ1\overline{q}:V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} constructed in §\lx@sectionsign 3.1.2. Indeed such an automorphism certainly preserves the conic CC and it maps the five (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves F1,…,F5F_{1},\ldots,F_{5} to five other (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves each intersecting CC transversally. But it follows from the construction of VV from ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} that F1,…,F5F_{1},\ldots,F_{5} are the only five (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves in VV with this property. Similarly, since LL and p=L∩Cp=L\cap C are Ψ\Psi-invariant, the image of TT by Ψ\Psi must be a smooth rational curve intersecting LL and CC transversally at pp but the construction of VV again implies that TT is the only curve in VV with this property. It follows that the divisors C+∑i=15FiC+\sum_{i=1}^{5}F_{i} and 3​T+L3T+L which generate the pencil q¯:V⇢ℙ1\overline{q}:V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} are Ψ\Psi-invariant whence that q¯\overline{q} is globally preserved by Ψ\Psi as claimed. This implies in turn that every automorphism φ\varphi of SS which extends to a biregular automorphism of the pair (V,D)\left(V,D\right) fits into a commutative diagram

Corollary 15, (b)), and SS carries two conjugated 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations q:S→ℙ1q:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} and q∘jGV,p:S→ℙ1q\circ j_{G_{V,p}}:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, each of these having no non trivial automorphism.

3.3. Automorphisms of special rational pencils


This subsection is devoted to the proof of the following result:

Proposition 17.

Let Q⊆ℙ3Q\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{3} be a smooth cubic surface and let ρ¯:ℙ3⇢ℙ1\overline{\rho}:\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} be the special pencil associated to a line L⊆QL\subseteq Q and a distinguished hyperplane H∈|𝒪ℙ3​(1)⊗ℐL|H\in\left|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{3}}(1)\otimes\mathcal{I}_{L}\right| as in §\lx@sectionsign 3.1.1. Then every automorphism of the induced rational fibration ρ:ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1\rho:\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} is the restriction of an automorphism of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}.

Proof.

Let us denote by Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho) the subgroup of Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q) consisting of automorphisms preserving the fibration ρ:ℙ3∖Q→𝔸1=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[λ])\rho:\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[\lambda]) fiberwise. Taking restriction over the generic point η\eta of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} induces an injective homomorphism from Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho) to the group Aut⁡(Sη)\mathrm{Aut}(S_{\eta}) of automorphisms of the generic fiber SηS_{\eta} of ρ\rho, and we identify from now on Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho) with its image in Aut⁡(Sη)\mathrm{Aut}(S_{\eta}). By definition, SηS_{\eta} is a nonsingular affine surface defined over the field ℂ⁡(λ)\mathbb{C}(\lambda) whose closure in ℙℂ⁡(λ)3\mathbb{P}_{\mathbb{C}(\lambda)}^{3} is a nonsingular cubic surface VηV_{\eta} such that Dη=Vη∖SηD_{\eta}=V_{\eta}\setminus S_{\eta} consists of either three lines LηL_{\eta}, Lη,1L_{\eta,1} and Lη,2L_{\eta,2} meeting a unique ℂ⁡(λ)\mathbb{C}(\lambda)-rational point or the union of a line LηL_{\eta} and nonsingular conic CηC_{\eta} intersecting LηL_{\eta} at a unique ℂ⁡(λ)\mathbb{C}(\lambda)-rational point pp. The same argument as in the proofs of Proposition 14 and its Corollary 15 implies that Aut⁡(Sη)=Aut⁡(Vη,Dη)\mathrm{Aut}(S_{\eta})=\mathrm{Aut}(V_{\eta},D_{\eta}) in the first case whereas Aut⁡(Sη)=Aut⁡(Vη,Dη)⋊ℤ2⋅jGVη,p\mathrm{Aut}(S_{\eta})=\mathrm{Aut}(V_{\eta},D_{\eta})\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cdot j_{G_{V_{\eta},p}}, where jGVη,pj_{G_{V_{\eta},p}} denotes the affine Geiser involution with the center at pp, in the second case. In the first case, we conclude that every automorphism of Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho) is generically of degree one when considered as a birational self-map of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} and hence is the restriction of an automorphism of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. So it remains to show that in the second case, one has Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)⊆Aut⁡(Vη,Dη)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{Aut}(V_{\eta},D_{\eta}) necessarily. Suppose on the contrary that Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)⊈Aut⁡(Vη,Dη)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho)\not\subseteq\mathrm{Aut}(V_{\eta},D_{\eta}). Then since we have an extension

0→Aut⁡(Vη,Dη)→Aut⁡(Sη)→ℤ2⋅jGVη,p→0,0\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(V_{\eta},D_{\eta})\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(S_{\eta})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{2}\cdot j_{G_{V_{\eta,p}}}\rightarrow 0,

it would follow that jGVη,p∈Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)j_{G_{V_{\eta,p}}}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho). On the other hand, letting πp:ℙ3⇢ℙ2\pi_{p}:\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} be the projection from the point pp, the rational map (ρ¯,πp):ℙ3⇢ℙ1×ℙ2(\overline{\rho},\pi_{p}):\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{2} is generically of degree 22, contracting the plane HH to a line πp​(H)∈ρ¯​(H)×ℙ2≃ℙ2\pi_{p}(H)\in\overline{\rho}(H)\times\mathbb{P}^{2}\simeq\mathbb{P}^{2} and inducing a Galois double covering

ℙ3∖(Q∪H)→ℙ1∖{ρ¯​(Q)∪ρ¯​(H)}×ℙ2∖(πp​(Q)∪πp​(H))≃𝔸∗1×𝔸2∖(πp​(Q)).\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus(Q\cup H)\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\left\{\overline{\rho}(Q)\cup\overline{\rho}(H)\right\}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus(\pi_{p}(Q)\cup\pi_{p}(H))\simeq\mathbb{A}_{*}^{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus(\pi_{p}(Q)).

By definition, the affine Geiser involution jGVη,pj_{G_{V_{\eta},p}} of SηS_{\eta} is simply the restriction to the generic fiber of ρ\rho of the nontrivial involution JJ of this covering. So jGVη,p∈Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)j_{G_{V_{\eta,p}}}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho) considered as a birational self-map of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} would coincide with JJ which is absurd since the latter contracts HH whence the fiber ρ−1​(ρ¯​(H))\rho^{-1}(\overline{\rho}(H)) of ρ\rho. Thus Aut⁡(ℙ3∖Q,ρ)⊆Aut⁡(Vη,Dη)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{3}\setminus Q,\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{Aut}(V_{\eta},D_{\eta}) as desired. ∎
